title: Read and change permissions
objective: By the end of this lesson you can decode any permission string on sight, set permissions deliberately with chmod, and explain why 777 is a finding rather than a fix.

blocks.text: This is where the filesystem and the user accounts from earlier lessons meet. Permissions are where the operating system's fourth job — deciding who may do what — becomes something you can read and change. It is also the single most common source of real-world misconfiguration findings.
Ten characters, three groups of three

blocks.caption: The permission string, split up
lines: |   |    +-------  group: members of the owning group
+----------------  type: - file, d directory, l link

blocks.text: Each group of three is always in the same order: r for read, w for write, x for execute. A dash means the permission is absent. So rw-r--r-- reads as: the owner may read and write; the group may read; everyone else may read.

rows: Create, rename, or delete entries inside
Enter it and reach things inside

blocks.title: The directory column surprises people
blocks.text: w on a directory means someone can delete files inside it — even files they do not own and cannot read. And without x on a directory you cannot reach anything inside, no matter what the permissions on those files say. Directory permissions gate the path, not just the folder.
The numbers are just the letters in binary
Each group of three is one digit. Read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1, and you add up whichever are present. That arithmetic is all there is to numeric modes.

items: 644 = rw-r--r--  — the normal setting for a document
755 = rwxr-xr-x  — the normal setting for a program or a directory
600 = rw-------  — owner only; correct for a private key or a secrets file

blocks.caption: Two ways to say the same thing
lines: chmod 644 notes.txt        # numeric: set exactly this
chmod u+x deploy.sh        # symbolic: add execute for the owner
chmod go-w shared/         # remove write from group and others
chmod -R 755 website/      # apply down a whole tree
chown songpon notes.txt          # change the owning user (needs sudo)
chown songpon:staff notes.txt    # change user and group

blocks.text: Numeric sets the whole state at once and is unambiguous. Symbolic adjusts one thing and leaves the rest alone. Use numeric when you know exactly what the end state should be; use symbolic when you are making one targeted change.

When something does not work, 777 makes the permission error go away. That is why it appears in so many forum answers and so many production systems. What it actually says is: any user and any process on this machine may read this, change it, and run it.

blocks.title: The realistic attack, in three steps
blocks.text: An attacker gets a foothold as a low-privileged account — say the web server user. They find a script that is 777 and that runs regularly as root. They edit the script, because 777 said they could. The next time it runs, their code runs as root. No exploit was involved. The permissions already allowed the edit.
The fix is almost never 777. It is to work out which user needs which access and grant that: usually correcting ownership with chown, or adding the right group, then setting 644 or 755.

blocks.title: Read one permission string
steps: Make a file with a known mode: printf 'x\n' > perm-lab.txt && chmod 640 perm-lab.txt
Before reading further, say out loud who can read it, who can write it, and who can do neither
Check yourself against the machine: stat -c '%A %U %G' perm-lab.txt   (macOS: stat -f '%Sp %Su %Sg' perm-lab.txt)
Now change one bit at a time and predict the string before each: chmod 644, then 600, then 755
For each, write the three-character group for owner, group and others before running ls -l
Finally: chmod 000 perm-lab.txt then try cat perm-lab.txt as yourself — explain the error you get
blocks.expected: A permission string you can read without hesitating, and one prediction you got wrong — usually 640, because people forget that the group digit is 4 and not 6. The chmod 000 step is the one worth sitting with: the owner of a file can still change its mode back, which is why 000 protects a file from everyone except the person who matters most.

blocks.title: Prove each rule to yourself
steps: Run: cd ~ && mkdir -p perm-lab && cd perm-lab
Run: echo 'hello' > secret.txt && ls -l secret.txt        (note the default permissions)
Run: chmod 600 secret.txt && ls -l secret.txt             (now owner-only)
Run: printf '#!/bin/sh\necho it ran\n' > run.sh && ./run.sh    (fails — no execute bit)
Run: chmod u+x run.sh && ./run.sh                          (now it runs)
Run: ls -ld .                                              (read the directory's own permissions)
blocks.expected: You see default permissions, tighten a file to owner-only, watch a script refuse to run and then run once it has x, and finally read the permissions on the directory itself rather than its contents.

cheatsheet: Ten characters: type, then user / group / others, each rwx
r read · w write · x execute (on a directory: list · modify contents · enter)
w on a directory lets someone delete files they do not own
Without x on a directory you cannot reach anything inside it
Numbers: r=4 w=2 x=1, added per group
644 documents · 755 programs and directories · 600 secrets · 777 never
chmod 644 file sets exactly; chmod u+x file adjusts one bit
chown user:group file changes ownership (usually needs sudo)
777 lets any process on the box rewrite the file — the classic escalation path
Fix permission errors with correct ownership and 644/755, not with 777

choices.A: Owner: read only · group: write · others: execute
choices.B: Everyone can read, write and execute
choices.C: Owner: read/write · group: read · others: read
choices.D: Owner rwx · group r-x · others none

checkpoint.explanation: Split it into three groups of three after the type character: rwx for the owner, r-x for the group, --- for everyone else.
6 = 4+2 = rw-, 4 = r--, 0 = ---. A common setting for a config file readable by a service group but by nobody else.

checkpoint.prompt: A colleague fixes a permission error by running chmod -R 777 on an application directory. What have they actually done?

choices.B: Every file rw and executable by all users
choices.D: Restricted the directory to the owner alone

checkpoint.explanation: 777 grants everything to everyone. Any compromised low-privilege process on that host can now rewrite those files, and whatever runs them afterwards runs the attacker's code. Readable, writable and executable — by every user and process on the machine.

checkpoint.prompt: You need a private key file to be readable only by its owner. Which command is correct?
checkpoint.explanation: 600 is rw------- — the owner may read and write, nobody else has any access. SSH will refuse to use a key that is more permissive than this.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can a user delete a file inside a directory even when they have no write permission on the file itself?

choices.A: Because the file was owned by root
choices.C: Deleting normally requires write and execute permission on the parent directory
choices.D: Because deletion pays no attention to permissions at all

checkpoint.explanation: Removing a name changes the containing directory. On Linux it normally requires write and execute (search) permission on that parent directory; write alone is insufficient when execute is absent. The file's own write bit does not control removal.

checkpoint.prompt: A directory grants you write and execute but not read permission. What can you normally do?

choices.A: Access a known name and create or remove entries, but not list all names
choices.B: List all names but not enter the directory
choices.C: Read every file in it regardless of file modes

checkpoint.explanation: For directories, read permits listing, write permits changing entries, and execute is search permission. Without read you cannot list names, but write plus search can still let you act on names you already know.

checkpoint.prompt: What exact change does chmod go-w shared/ make?

choices.A: Adds write permission to group and others
choices.B: Removes write permission from group and others

checkpoint.explanation: The user classes g and o mean group and others; - removes the named permission. The command leaves the owner's permissions and every read or execute bit unchanged.

checkpoint.prompt: A directory has mode 750. What may a member of its owning group do?

choices.B: Write names but not search it
choices.C: List and search it but not create or remove entries

checkpoint.explanation: 750 is rwx for owner, r-x for group, and --- for others. Group members can list and traverse the directory but lack its write permission, so they cannot create or remove names there.

checkpoint.prompt: What does chown alice:ops report.txt request?

choices.C: Copy report.txt to alice's home directory
choices.D: Set its owner to alice and group to ops

checkpoint.explanation: chown changes ownership. The user before the colon is the owner and the group after it is the owning group; permission to make that change normally requires appropriate privilege.

checkpoint.prompt: A shell script is readable but ./run.sh returns Permission denied. Which missing mode bit is the direct cause?
checkpoint.explanation: A regular file needs execute permission to be run as a program. chmod u+x run.sh changes only the owner's execute bit, preserving its other mode bits.

checkpoint.prompt: After chmod 000 secret.txt, why can the file's owner usually restore access with chmod 600 secret.txt?

choices.B: The owner may change the mode of their file
choices.D: The group automatically receives write access

checkpoint.explanation: Mode bits control ordinary access, while the file owner is normally permitted to change them. This is why 000 is not protection from the account that owns the file.

checkpoint.prompt: A file is currently 777. What is true after chmod 644 file?

choices.B: The owner keeps execute because it was already set
choices.C: The mode is set exactly to rw-r--r--
choices.D: The command changes ownership as well

checkpoint.explanation: A numeric mode sets all three permission groups exactly. 644 gives owner read/write and group and others read-only; it does not preserve the previous execute bits.

checkpoint.prompt: You can read /srv/app/config.ini itself, but opening that known path fails because you lack execute permission on /srv/app. What is missing?

choices.D: Search permission needed to traverse the directory

checkpoint.explanation: Execute on a directory is search permission. Without it, a user cannot traverse the directory to reach an entry, even when the entry's own read mode would otherwise allow reading.

checkpoint.prompt: A root-run deployment job executes /opt/app/deploy.sh. Why is making that script world-writable dangerous?

choices.A: Any local account can replace code that root will later run
choices.B: It prevents root from reading the script
choices.C: It makes the script run only once

checkpoint.explanation: Write permission determines who may alter the file. If an untrusted account can change a script that a privileged job executes, the job executes that account's code with its own privileges.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is chmod -R 755 documents/ a poor default fix for an ordinary document tree?

choices.B: It adds execute permission to every regular file as well
choices.C: It removes all owner write permission
choices.D: It changes every file owner to root

checkpoint.explanation: Recursive chmod applies the specified mode to directories and their contents. Directories need search permission, but ordinary documents generally do not need to become executable; choose modes by role instead of one blanket number.
